claims.claim: Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus
claims.note: NASA: "Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune." No later mission has reached Uranus as of 2026-11-17. Jasinski abstract also calls it "This single in situ measurement".

claims.claim: ... and it arrived at an unusual time.
claims.source_checked: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-024-02389-3 (doi:10.1038/s41550-024-02389-3, full text via Firecrawl), abstract and Conclusions
claims.note: Abstract: Voyager 2 saw the magnetosphere "in an anomalous, compressed state that we estimate to be present less than 5% of the time". Conclusions: "We have demonstrated that Voyager 2 observed the Uranian magnetosphere during a highly atypical and compressed state". The authors state it as shown, so a flat 'unusual time' does not overstate. A viewer who swipes at second two leaves with two true statements: one visitor, and its timing was unusual. Unusual in what way is left open, which is not a falsehood.
NASA: "Closest approach to Uranus took place at 17:59 UT Jan. 24, 1986". Jasinski: inbound bow shock 24 January 1986 07:28 UT, magnetopause ~10:07 UT the same day.

claims.claim: In the days before, the solar wind had picked up and squeezed the magnetic bubble around the planet.
claims.note: Body: "both the density and dynamic pressure were steadily increasing for 2 days (including a modest increase in v) before the flyby, from ~0.005 nPa to 0.018 nPa". Conclusions: "The magnetosphere of Uranus was continuously compressed (from ~28 to ~17 R_U) for the days leading up to the Voyager 2 flyby". 'Picked up' is fair: pressure, density and (modestly) speed all rose. 'Magnetic bubble' = magnetosphere. The line attributes only the compression to the solar wind, not the field's tilt/offset, which matches the paper.

claims.claim: Researchers estimate it is squeezed that hard only about four percent of the time.
claims.source_checked: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-024-02389-3 (Main, para. after Fig. 2; Fig. 3 caption; abstract)
claims.note: Body: "a Voyager 2-observed magnetopause R_SS of 17.3 R_U or lower is expected to occur only 4% of the time at Uranus"; Fig. 3: "expected only 4% of the time"; abstract "less than 5%". 'Researchers estimate' keeps the hedge. Caveat for the record, not a fix: the distribution is built from Voyager 2's own solar-wind data while it crossed Uranus's orbital distance (DOY 290 1985 to DOY 158 1986, solar minimum); the paper itself states the 4% generally, so the present tense matches the source.

claims.claim: Had Voyager arrived a few days earlier, the solar wind pressing on it would have been about twenty times weaker.
claims.note: The abstract does say "only a few days earlier ... ~20 times lower", but the paper's own data contradict that pairing. A few (2) days earlier the pressure was ~0.005 nPa, "an almost fourfold increase from day 22", i.e. ~4x, not 20x. The ~20x ("~18 to ~23 times lower") values are 0.001 nPa "eight days before the flyby" and the 0.00078 nPa minimum on day 13 (11 days before); days 16-21 are a data gap. The Conclusions say "Had Voyager 2 arrived at Uranus a week earlier ... much weaker solar wind dynamic pressure". Per A3 take the narrower, data-backed reading. Change to e.g. 'Had Voyager arrived about a week earlier, the solar wind pushing on that bubble would have been about twenty times weaker.' (or keep 'a few days' with 'about four times weaker'). Also fix the pronoun: 'pressing on it' follows 'Voyager', so listeners hear the solar wind pressing on the spacecraft; name the bubble. Update SOURCES entry 6 to cite the eight-day/day-13 figures and note the abstract's looser wording.

claims.claim: So the extreme Uranus we have described for forty years may just be what one unusual few days looked like.
claims.note: The hedge matches (abstract: "the interpretation of Uranus's magnetosphere as being extreme may simply be a product of a flyby that occurred under extreme upstream solar wind conditions"), and 1986 to 2026 is forty years. But the spoken line says 'the extreme Uranus', not its magnetosphere. Uranus is famous as extreme for things the paper does not touch (sideways spin, and the 'unusually oblique and off-centred magnetic field', which the paper treats as real and says its result is 'unlikely to change the conclusions of Connerney et al.'). A listener can hear that Uranus's strangeness in general may be an artefact: overstates the source (A3). The SOURCES block limits the scope only for visuals; the spoken words need it too. Change to e.g. 'So the extreme magnetic bubble we have described for forty years may just be what one unusual stretch of days looked like.' Optional: 'few days' is loose against the ~8 days of compression (~28 to ~17 R_U) the paper describes; 'one unusual week' would match claim 6 if that is changed to 'a week'.
